The word nimbus has two core, distinct meanings — one from the world of art and religion, and one from weather science. There is also a third, more general figurative use.
Meaning 1: A Halo — A Circle of Light Around a Sacred Figure

This is the oldest and most visually striking meaning.

A nimbus is the glowing circle or disk of light depicted around the head of a divine, holy, or sacred figure in paintings, sculptures, and religious artwork. Think of classic images of Jesus, the Virgin Mary, the Buddha, angels, or Hindu gods — they are very commonly shown with a bright golden ring hovering around their heads. That ring is a nimbus.

You may know this concept better by the word halo, and yes, the two words are often used interchangeably in everyday language. However, "nimbus" is the older, more formal, and more technically precise term — the one scholars, art historians, and theologians prefer.

Why does this symbol exist? The nimbus visually signals to the viewer that this figure is not an ordinary human. They are sacred, spiritually elevated, or connected to a higher power. Light, across nearly all cultures and religions, is universally associated with goodness, purity, truth, and divinity. The nimbus captures this symbolism by literally placing a glow of light around a holy person's head.

The nimbus appears across many cultures and traditions:

  • In Christianity — around Jesus Christ, the Virgin Mary, saints, and angels
  • In Buddhism — around the Buddha and Bodhisattvas (enlightened beings)
  • In Hinduism — around gods such as Vishnu and Krishna
  • In ancient Roman and Greek art — around emperors and deities

Art historians also distinguish between different shapes of nimbus:

  • A circular nimbus (a round ring) is by far the most common, used for saints and holy figures generally
  • A cruciform nimbus (a ring with a cross inside it) was reserved specifically for Christ in Christian art
  • A triangular nimbus was sometimes used for God the Father, representing the Holy Trinity
  • A square nimbus was occasionally used in early Christian art for living people regarded as holy — not yet dead or officially sainted

This meaning of nimbus is the one you'll most often encounter in museums, religious texts, and art history discussions.

The second meaning of nimbus belongs to weather science.

In meteorology, nimbus refers to a dark, heavy cloud that produces precipitation — meaning rain, snow, sleet, or hail. When the sky turns a deep, threatening gray and heavy clouds roll in before a downpour, those are the kinds of clouds the word "nimbus" historically described.

In modern cloud science, "nimbus" almost never stands alone as a cloud classification. Instead, it appears as part of compound cloud names, where it contributes the meaning of "rain-producing" or "precipitation-bearing":

Nimbostratus — This is a thick, dark gray, blanket-like layer of cloud that spreads across the entire sky. It brings steady, prolonged rain or snow — not a dramatic storm, but the kind of persistent, all-day drizzle that makes everything feel gray and damp. The prefix "nimbo" signals rain; "stratus" means it lies in flat, horizontal layers.

Cumulonimbus — This is the dramatic one. It is a massive, towering thunderstorm cloud, the tallest cloud that forms in the atmosphere. A fully developed cumulonimbus can stretch from near the ground all the way to the top of the troposphere. It produces heavy rain, lightning, thunder, hail, powerful winds, and sometimes tornadoes. "Cumulo" refers to its heaped, billowing shape; "nimbus" tells you it means serious weather.

So whenever you see "nimb-" or "-nimbus" in a cloud name, it is always signalling: this cloud brings precipitation.
Meaning 3: An Aura or Surrounding Atmosphere (Figurative Use)

Beyond art and weather, "nimbus" also appears in general and literary language to describe an intangible aura, atmosphere, or invisible quality that seems to surround a person, place, or thing — much like a cloud envelops something.

For example:

  • A powerful political leader might be said to carry a nimbus of authority — meaning they seem to radiate an invisible sense of commanding importance.
  • A haunted old house might be described as wrapped in a nimbus of dread — an atmosphere of unease you can feel but not see.
  • A legendary artist might be surrounded by a nimbus of mystique — a sense of something special and untouchable that defines how the world perceives them.

In this sense, "nimbus" is a poetic or literary word that works like a metaphor. It borrows from both its other meanings — the glowing light around a holy figure, and the enveloping quality of a cloud — to describe an invisible but very real "atmosphere" clinging to something or someone.

To summarize everything in plain terms:

A nimbus is, depending on the context, one of three things. In art and religion, it is the halo or glowing ring of light placed around the head of a sacred figure to mark them as holy. In meteorology, it is a dark, rain-bearing cloud, most commonly seen in compound terms like nimbostratus and cumulonimbus. And in figurative language, it is the aura or invisible atmosphere of some quality that seems to surround a person or thing.

What connects all three meanings is a shared core idea: something surrounding, enveloping, or radiating outward from a central subject — whether that's divine light, rain clouds, or an intangible aura of personality or power.
